name: Omita Khar
subtitle: the alkaline assamese opener — raw papaya simmered soft, plain and cleansing

ingredients.qty: 500g, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm cubes

ingredients.note: stands in for khar, the alkaline water filtered through sun-dried banana-peel ash; the catalogue has no khar and this is the standard urban substitute
fried till golden, the upper-Assam habit

prepNotes: A quarter teaspoon of baking soda is the ceiling for this quantity. More and the dish turns soapy and slippery on the tongue — there is no fixing it once it is in.
Soak the whole urad 30 minutes and drain it thoroughly on a cloth, or it will spit in the hot oil.
Khar is eaten first, at the very start of an Assamese meal, with plain rice and nothing sour alongside it.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pan until it smokes, then let it cool for a minute.
Fry the drained urad 2 minutes until deep gold and lift it out with a slotted spoon. Keep it for the end.
steps.tip: It should crackle, not brown in seconds — if it darkens instantly the oil is still too hot.

steps.text: Drop in the slit chillies and let them blister 30 seconds.
Add the papaya, turmeric and salt and toss 3 minutes, until the cut edges look glassy.
Pour in the water, cover and simmer 12 minutes, until a fork goes through a cube with no resistance.
Stir in the baking soda and simmer uncovered 5 minutes. It will foam up and settle, and the liquid turns faintly silky.
steps.tip: Add it at the end, never at the start — early alkali collapses the papaya to mush.

steps.text: Crush four or five cubes against the side of the pan to thicken the broth, then scatter over the fried urad and coriander and serve at once.

storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, and the alkali keeps softening the papaya, so it will be looser on day two. Reheat gently with a splash of water; add the fried urad fresh if you want the crunch back.
